extracted.intended_audience: lawmakers, legislators, and politically engaged readers considering constitutional design (originally addressed to British Parliamentarians and the educated public)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracting normative criteria for assessing the quality and stability of a constitution (legislative, executive, judicial, and military design), with particular attention to features that promote continuity, authority, and protection of liberty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve local attachments and provincial identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Political organization should respect habitual provincial connections and local attachments rather than imposing artificial geometric divisions ('one country, one heart, and one Assembly' by square measurement).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke argues that public affections begin in families and neighborhoods; governments that erase traditional local divisions risk removing the attachments that train citizens to care for the larger polity. Anti-pattern: imposing uniform, arbitrary territorial units will weaken social cohesion and patriotism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Existence of an intermediate council or senate
rubrics_metrics.description: A republican constitution should include a senate or like council — a body between the supreme popular assembly and the executive — to give steadiness, consistency, and a point of foreign connection.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Such a body supplies bias and steadiness, preserves consistency in state proceedings, and serves roles analogous to councils in monarchies. Omitting it is termed by Burke a 'sovereign incapacity' of framers of constitutions without such a council.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberative executive with real discretion
rubrics_metrics.description: The executive should not be a mere machine or channel but must possess deliberative discretion and means to reward and sustain authority; an impotent, purely executory officer degrades the office and cannot command obedience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke criticizes an executive made only to transmit information to the legislature and deprived of prerogatives (originating justice, suspension, pardon, rewards). Guidance: ensure executive has dignity, authority, and material means (offices, pensions, honors) to induce loyal service; anti-pattern: an executive reduced to 'bumbailiffs, sergeants-at-mace' whose functions are only odious coercion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executive as fountain of justice and honor
rubrics_metrics.description: A legitimate executive should be the source of justice and honors in the polity; removing these roles from the executive reduces respect for the office and undermines its effectiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke notes that when judges and public prosecutions are detached from the executive, and when all rewards/distinctions are elsewhere, the executive has no natural motive to command service except fear. Good design restores some prerogatives to the executive or compensating auxiliary trusts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ministers must have dignity, independence, and effective authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Ministers of state should be empowered, honored, and selected for ability (by affairs not affections); they must have the means to act and retain authority to serve the state loyally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke warns that ministers who are 'forced upon' a humiliated executive will create mutual counteraction; ministers require a tolerable share in councils and the prospect of glory or reward to act zealously. Anti-pattern: ministers who are responsible but lack discretion or protection become ineffective and perpetually vulnerable to assaults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate executive prerogatives in foreign policy (peace and war)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some dangerous but necessary prerogatives (notably the right of peace and war) may need to be vested in the executive to prevent personal intrigues between foreign potentates and legislators that would foment pernicious factions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke suggests delegating this prerogative carefully (ideally coupled with auxiliary trusts) as a means to keep foreign sovereigns from personally intriguing with members of the legislature; if not given to the monarch, other indirect correctives and controls must be designed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent, permanent judiciary (insulated from local faction)
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges should be constituted with permanence and independence (life tenure / near inheritance) and not be elective, temporary, or narrowly local, because dependent/sessional tribunals invite faction and partiality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke praises the old parliaments' independence and permanence as safeguards of law and property. Anti-patterns: sexennial elective judicatories, short-term local judges who will be biased against strangers, minorities, and the wealthy; ballots that create suspicion rather than concealment of inclinations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicature exterior to the supreme power to balance it
rubrics_metrics.description: The supreme power of the state ought to be balanced by a judicature that is in some sense exterior to the state, providing security for justice against political power.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke argues that something 'exterior to the state' helps secure justice and property; courts should act as corrective to transient democratic decrees. Practical guidance: locate high courts and structures so they are not merely instruments of the current majority.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve remonstrance/registration functions to check legislative excess
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be a body (e.g., parliaments or courts of remonstrance) empowered to register and remonstrate upon decrees of the legislative assembly to square them with general jurisprudence and prevent rule by occasional decrees (psephismata).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke laments abolishing the parliaments' remonstrance role. Use remonstrance to convert occasional decrees into legally consistent principles; anti-pattern: vesting remonstrance in the executing officer (king) who is subordinate to the assembly and thus incapable of a genuine check.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid rule by frequent occasional decrees (psephismata)
rubrics_metrics.description: Governments must avoid constant governance by ad hoc decrees; reliance on 'occasional decrees' undermines legal consistency, public respect for law, and ultimately destroys the rule of law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke points out ancient democracies fell because they governed by intermittent decrees; guidance is to create stable, general, and coherent codes rather than ephemeral measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial independence from legislative instructions and changing rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Judges must not be sworn to obey rules, orders, and instructions from the legislature that can change the rule of decision in the midst of causes; doing so makes judges instruments of governing power and destroys legal ground for subjects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke condemns constitutions that appoint judges and then reserve to the Assembly the right to provide the law later; practical rule: judges must decide according to established law and learning, not ad hoc legislative commands that can be applied retroactively or capriciously.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative bodies accountable to law (not exempted)
rubrics_metrics.description: Administrative and executive corporations that execute public pecuniary trusts must be subject to legal coercion and judicial oversight; exempting them places them above law and corrupts accountability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke notes administrative bodies were carefully exempted from jurisdiction in the French plan, making them instruments for oligarchy. Good design: allow legal tribunals (like King's Bench or equivalent) to coerce corporate officers and offer protection to those executing lawful corporate functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: High court of justice must be independent and not subservient to inquisition
rubrics_metrics.description: A grand state judicature that judges crimes against the nation must be formed in a spirit different from inquisitionary committees; it must not try causes of its own members at pleasure nor be seated in the same political republic as the dominant assembly (avoid locating it in Paris alone).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke warns that if this tribunal is subservient to the Committee of Research it will extinguish liberty. Practical guidance: remove prosecution of political offenses from the immediate control of the assembly and consider locating the court where it is less exposed to popular inquisition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Army discipline subordinated to civilian authority; prevent military democracy
rubrics_metrics.description: The army must remain an instrument under civilian authority, with discipline and subordination; if the military becomes a deliberative body, the state degenerates into a 'military democracy' which devours its creators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke stresses the necessity that the army 'should never act but as an instrument.' Design must secure chains of command, authority of commanders, courts-martial and penal enforcement. Anti-pattern: permitting regimental committees, popular soldier assemblies, or tolerating the murder of commandants with impunity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide effective means to enforce military discipline
rubrics_metrics.description: Respond decisively to military insurrections with proper courts, martial law where necessary, and inquiry/punishment for crimes (e.g., murder of commanders) rather than relying only on proclamations and additional oaths.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke criticizes the Assembly's response of more decrees and oaths instead of actual coercive measures. Practical measures: civil/military courts, breaking mutinous corps, decimation or equivalent legal punishments, and clear enforcement mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legislation clarity vs judicial learning: avoid hollow 'short laws'
rubrics_metrics.description: Laws should be substantive, clear, and supported by legal learning; overly 'short' laws that leave much to judicial discretion while devaluing legal learning will produce unsound discretion and instability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke notes the Assembly promises to form laws 'short, simple, clear' but warns that such brevity can leave too much to judges without legal learning. Guidance: balance legislative clarity with respect for legal expertise rather than substituting vagueness for learned jurisprudence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design offices and honors to motivate faithful executive service
rubrics_metrics.description: To secure zealous and faithful performance by executors and subordinates, the constitution should supply offices, grants, pensions, or honors — material and moral incentives — otherwise service will be motivated solely by fear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burke observes that where the executive cannot grant rewards, those who serve him have no natural motive but fear. Good constitutional design provides means of reward to encourage energetic and loyal execution of duties.
